item.title: Specialized High School Test Crashes, Rattling Students Across New York
item.description:
Some New York City students hoping to gain entry to one of the city’s exclusive high schools next fall hit a snag on Saturday when the online system used for the admissions test failed.

The Specialized High School Admissions Test, or SHSAT, is the sole admissions criterion for the city’s eight specialized high schools, which include Stuyvesant High School and the Bronx High School of Science.

A note handed to parents who picked up their children from one of the testing sites at Brooklyn Technical High School in Fort Greene said that the “testing sites experienced a technical issue” and so “testing was discontinued.”

The New York City Department of Education later said in a statement that “the vendor experienced technical issue with the testing platform that kept many students from accessing and finishing the test,” and so the exam was rescheduled. The department did not say how many students were affected. Pearson, the vendor of the exam, did not respond to a request for comment.

“Every student who was unable to finish will be automatically rescheduled, and testing on a new date will not affect any student’s score or consideration for admission to a specialized high school,” the statement read. “We apologize for the disruption and are working with the vendor to ensure this is fixed and does not happen again.”

According to the D.O.E., approximately 30,000 eighth graders and 5,000 ninth graders take the test each year. The test went online in 2025, a switch from paper tests, and was scheduled this year for Nov. 14, 15 and 21, as well as an in-school testing day on Nov. 18. It was unclear whether future test days would be affected.

Specialized schools educate only about 5 percent of New York City high schoolers.

“This is a pretty complicated, deep exam and everybody gets psyched for today,” said Gregory Comeau, 67, a New York City tutor who has roughly 25 students taking the SHSAT this year. “It’s an emotional thing, and this has to be a letdown.”

It was unclear how many testing sites were impacted on Saturday and how many students would have to retake the test. According to the note given to parents, students who were scheduled to sit for the exam on Saturday would be given a new testing date by Friday, Nov. 20.

Students who were unable to take the test on Nov. 14 will automatically be rescheduled, while any child who completed testing but felt that it was disrupted by the technical difficulties could request a retest, the note said.

Two years ago, the Panel for Educational Policy, a New York City education group, approved a new five-year, $17 million contract with the education publisher Pearson to administer the SHSAT. The test has been a major point of debate in the city for several years. Some see the exam as an opportunity to attend the city’s best schools, while others view it as a contributing factor to school segregation. During his run for mayor last year, Zohran Mamdani said, “We have the most segregated school system in America,” referring to a 2014 finding from the Civil Rights Project at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Kyisha Brooks-Robinson, 45, said that her daughter, Skyla Robinson, sat down to take the test at Brooklyn Technical High School at 8:30 a.m. on Saturday, but the computer took until 10 a.m. to produce the test. She began her math section but was interrupted a short time later when a proctor came in to tell the students in the classroom that they would all be rescheduled.

Ms. Brooks-Robinson said that because Skyla had been able to start the test, her name was designated with an asterisk in the record to ensure she would take an entirely new test the next time around since she got through only two questions.

Skyla was worried that the retake might be harder as a result, her mom said. The rescheduling was also a blow to Skyla, Ms. Brooks-Robinson said, because she had been taking SHSAT study classes twice a week in preparation.

“This test is really stressful for the kids,” Ms. Brooks-Robinson said. “All of the ‘good luck, wish you well, this is going to be a great thing,’ and all of a sudden they cannot take it.”

Ms. Brooks-Robinson said she had suffered outages at work this week when Microsoft went down. That, plus the Federal Aviation Administration’s ground stop on Friday night, made her think the district should be prepared for technical difficulties for the test.

“They should have paper tests on hand, considering everything that is happening,” she said.

Mr. Comeau, the tutor, said that in the competitive environment of specialized high schools in the city, students would roll with the punches of a rescheduled test.

“That’s part of the New York City life,” he said. “Admissions is a nightmare. It’s so unique here the way it works.”

item.title: They Want to Be Doctors. Student Loan Caps Are Complicating Their Dreams.
item.description:
Bryan Torres didn’t meet many doctors growing up. It wasn’t until he was 15, when his mother was hospitalized with respiratory failure, that he realized he wanted to be a physician.

Mr. Torres, who grew up in Maryvale, Ariz., and is of Mexican and Colombian descent, would translate between his mother and her doctors. They didn’t speak enough Spanish “to comfort my mom,” he recalled, and “didn’t look like me.”

Though Mr. Torres, now 33, said his mother received quality care, he felt “alienated, hopeless and helpless” while in the hospital with her.

“That’s kinda when I decided I wanted to dedicate my life to making sure that no one has to ever feel the way I felt in that moment,” he said.

After receiving his bachelor’s degree in biosystems engineering from the University of Arizona, he spent six years taking the medical school admissions exam five times, earning a master’s degree and working across the health field as a pharmacy technician, a medical assistant, an E.R. scribe, a molecular biologist and more.

In 2021, he was accepted to the Tulane School of Medicine with the intention of becoming a reconstructive plastic surgeon.

Now, in his last semester, his plans are in jeopardy.

Before his final semester, Mr. Torres received an email from Tulane telling him he was no longer eligible to take out federal loans to pay for medical school.

Under President Trump’s sweeping policy bill passed last year, professional students, like those in law and medicine programs, are not allowed to take out more than $50,000 a year in federal loans, with a total cap of $200,000. Federal loans for graduate programs like masters and Ph.D. programs were capped at $20,500 per year and a total of $100,000.

Education costs that are not covered by federal loans must be paid for using other funds. Most students use private loans, which often charge higher interest rates, have less flexible repayment options and fewer forgiveness options.

Mr. Torres was enrolled in medical school before the bill’s conception. But because he has already taken out over $257,500 in loans, he has reached the lifetime cap for federal borrowing.

Rather than take out private loans, Mr. Torres started a GoFundMe page and raised over $30,000 of the $50,000 he estimates he’ll need to finish school. When he’s not in clinical rotations, he has been driving for Uber and working for Rover, a pet care company.

Some of the money will help cover the cost of flights to about 20 cities for in-person interviews for residency programs across the country.

Despite these setbacks, Mr. Torres said he was still committed to becoming a doctor, though he said the loan caps could create wider disparities in representation in the field.

“Now it’s like, if you don’t have the money, and you don’t come from an affluent background, then therefore this profession is not meant for you,” he said.

This fall, a new class of medical school hopefuls is facing new rules on how much they can borrow for their educations.

The Department of Education cited the rising cost of college programs with “minimal or negative return on investment” as a reason for putting in place the loan caps signed into law. It added that “unrestricted borrowing has enabled institutions to raise tuition and fees without sufficient constraint, contributing to rising student loan debt.”

But schools are unlikely to lower their tuition rates simply because of loan caps.

Justin McAllister, the chief financial officer of the West Virginia School of Osteopathic Medicine, said it would be “impossible to be able to drive tuition down with inflation and the cost.”

Dr. Eva Aagaard, vice chancellor and vice dean for education at Washington University School of Medicine, agreed.

“There’s a misunderstanding broadly about how much it costs to train medical students and that medical schools could just reduce their tuition,” she said. “If we reduce our tuition, that money has to come from somewhere else.”

Dr. Aagaard and Mr. McAllister said their schools were trying to find ways to support students affected by the loan caps. Dr. Aagaard pointed toward the school’s scholarship program as an example. Nearly three-fourths of incoming students had full-tuition funding in 2025, but Dr. Aagaard acknowledged well-funded scholarships were not always available at every medical school.

Mr. McAllister said West Virginia formed partnerships with private lenders like AACOM by Sallie Mae, Citizens and SoFi to offer loans that didn’t require a co-signer, loans that had lower interest rates or loans that could be deferred through residency.

SoFi, for example, offers uncapped loan amounts with interest rates that vary between 2.99 percent and 15.33 percent (the interest rate for federal loans is 8.07 percent for graduate and professional students).

Mr. McAllister said loan caps “forced us to find our own options and create our own options.”

The Department of Education did not respond to a request for comment.

When Kiley Cleland was 19, she worked in clinics treating human trafficking survivors and “saw all these patients slipping through the cracks of how terrible our health care system was.”

“It was heartbreaking,” she said.

Her path to becoming a doctor has been difficult. She attended a community college initially because she didn’t have the grades to get into a four-year university. After transferring to the University of California, Davis, she was diagnosed with cervical dystonia, a neurological condition affecting the brain and nerves that left her with chronic pain, forcing her to drop out.

After getting her health back on track, she re-enrolled in her undergraduate program and finished with strong grades. She went on to receive her masters in bioethics at Johns Hopkins.

Now 27, Ms. Cleland is $85,000 in debt — a grant-funded program that she had planned to use toward her medical education fell through — and she has limited options. Though her medical school application is mostly ready, she delayed submitting it for another year because she said she felt financially insecure because of the loan caps.

To Ms Cleland, the government’s decision to apply the caps says: “If you’re rich, pursue medicine, be a doctor. And if you’re not, stop. Give up, go away.”

She doesn’t want to take out private loans but will consider them.

“I am the most relentless, hopeful, resilient, stubborn person there is,” Ms. Cleland said. “Which means I’m gonna grin and bear it.”

Researches have studied the long-term effects of loan caps on the field of medicine and health care system.

Dr. Tarun Ramesh, a research fellow at the Department of Population Medicine at Harvard Medical School, conducted a study published in 2025 examining how medical school costs had changed over time, and the potential impacts from capping education loans.

Dr. Ramesh and his team used data from the national postsecondary student financial aid survey and the Consumer Price Index to understand how much debt medical students were taking on, and how they were paying it back. He found that nearly half of medical students exceeded $50,000 in annual federal loans in 2020, and the annual cost of attendance, which includes tuition, fees, housing and food, had increased significantly over the prior decade.

That trend hasn’t slowed. College Tuition Compare, a website for tuition data, found that the average annual cost of attendance this year for medical school was almost $100,000.

Dr. Ramesh said that it’s unlikely students could afford medical school on $50,000 per year in federal loans, and that poorer students were more likely to exceed the lifetime cap.

The United States is projected to be short of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, with almost half of those open roles being for primary care physicians, according to a report from the Association of American Medical Colleges, or AAMC.

Primary care, along with pediatrics, are among the lowest-paid specialties in medicine. Dr. Ramesh said specialties like these were at bigger risk for a worsened shortage.

“I’m concerned that the O.B.B.B.A. restrictions may disincentivize medical students from engaging or going into primary care specialties,” he said, referring to Mr. Trump’s policy bill.

Kristen Earle, director of student financial services at AAMC, wrote in an email that she was “deeply concerned” the bill would “create significant financial barriers for medical students — especially those from low-income, rural and nontraditional backgrounds.”

Aquila Ali, a math major in her last year at New York University, grew up taking care of her younger brother. As he grew older, she noticed a behavioral shift in him.

After many doctor visits, and misdiagnoses, Ms. Ali’s brother was diagnosed with autism. She said her experience “seeing how doctors diagnose autism in children, especially Black children” was the start of her interest in becoming a physician-scientist.

Her original plan was to save up money during gap years and take out federal loans for medical school. But since Ms. Ali discovered she’d have to take out private loans to afford the full cost of medical school, she said she put those plans on the back burner.

“The more research I did, the more I realized that it would probably not be very realistic for me to go to medical school within the time frame that I wanted to,” she said. “Just because I just wouldn’t have enough money.”

Ms. Ali said she was planning on pursuing her Ph.D., but she still wanted to be a physician one day.

“I know that there’s still a place for me whether or not the federal government thinks so,” she said.

item.title: TikTok U
item.description:
Football players aren’t the only college students who have learned to sell their images for profit. At several universities, students can now major in content creation. In a recent survey, nearly four in 10 Gen Z respondents said they would take a million social media followers over a steady 9-to-5 job.

For a story in The Times today, I profiled someone who’s working on it. Meet Haley DeKreek, a 20-year-old junior at the University of Arizona. With more than 45,000 TikTok followers, a gift for self-deprecating humor, a talent manager in Los Angeles and several paid brand deals (the biggest so far worth $3,000), DeKreek says she can now pay for all her shopping, food, vacations and beauty services just by doing what she has loved since kindergarten, when she played with her mom’s makeup and recorded videos of herself making slime.

DeKreek lives in the Alpha Phi sorority house, a Spanish-colonial-style mansion just off campus in Tucson that is decorated in pale pink velvets and artful stacks of coffee table books about fashion. (Kourtney Kardashian, Arizona class of 2002, was also in Alpha Phi.)

Just off the foyer, a mailroom overflows with packages. There are boxes with yoga sets and dresses for formals, boxes of makeup, hair products and skin care. Many of them are destined to appear in the “Get Ready With Me” videos DeKreek regularly posts. And a lot of them are freebies from brands that have spotted her potential as a budding influencer, a one-girl campus marketing powerhouse.

DeKreek doesn’t formally study content creation in college, but her major, retail and consumer science, is entirely online; she never attends class in person.

I met DeKreek last month in the days before Arizona’s homecoming football game against Iowa State. It was a big week: Alumni had returned to campus, and fraternities and sororities threw events almost every night in the run-up to game day. She had a lot to do, beauty- and workwise, and I followed her around as she prepared.

Wednesday: Eyelash lift and tint, brow lamination, spray tan. Americans have spent the last year agog at male looksmaxxers, who hammer their own jaws and inject dubious substances in the name of beauty. But women have been practicing time-consuming, expensive, invasive and potentially self-destructive interventions for a long, long time. And they’re starting younger than ever: twentysomethings get Botox, teenagers get filler and preteens buy anti-aging skin care products.

At 20, DeKreek says she has already had lip filler and breast reduction surgery (her large chest made everyday activities physically painful). There have also been multiple rounds of Botox in her forehead (to keep her eyebrows level), cheeks (to stop nighttime jaw-clenching), armpits (to stop sweating) and upper lip. She has a hairstylist for her extensions and a friend who gives her regular spray tans. Now an aesthetician gives her an eyebrow-smoothing treatment and then perma-curls her lashes.

Thursday: Skin care, wellness walk. DeKreek starts every day by applying six of the skin care products stored in a white mini-fridge on her vanity — the first half of her routine. Then she and her friend Lea Gorham power-walk through campus, each sporting under-eye patches that are supposed to brighten and de-puff the skin there. Gorham is debating whether to get lip filler or just a cheaper lip flip. She doesn’t like the way she smiles. “I don’t necessarily need it, but it’s, like, everyone else at this school has it,” she says.

Both procedures are available at a local med spa, where undergraduates can use CatCash — student bursary funds, generally replenished by parents — to pay for any noninjectable beauty service by swiping their student IDs.

Next comes a blowout before DeKreek and her friends get ready for “Greek wedding,” an annual tradition where sororities and fraternities stage mock weddings between senior girls and senior boys, complete with funny speeches and parties. She spends three hours prepping: hair, makeup, body glow, dress, jewelry. The next day brings DeKreek’s monthly facial.

DeKreek herself has never had a boyfriend. She describes college hookup culture and the dates she has been set up on as a “waste of time.” “I just want to focus on myself,” she said, “and the right one will come along at some point.” It’s a common sentiment among young women, who have fewer romantic relationships than those in past generations.

Saturday. It’s time for the big game. DeKreek and her roommate deftly paint, blend, dab, brush, spray and dry their faces. Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Christina Aguilera sing from a speaker. The roommates’ friends burst in without knocking to rummage through their wardrobes, needing to borrow cutoffs and jewelry. DeKreek slides on a strapless gingham-and-lace mini-dress. Everyone is wearing identical tan knee-high boots, clomping to and fro.

This is what she means when she says, tenderly, “It’s like girlhood, all of us together.”

item.title: Why Public College Is Becoming Unaffordable
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Rents Are Pushing Cost of State Schools Over $50,000” (news article, Oct. 25):

The rising cost of higher education is a story about housing. And it isn’t just University of California students who are suffering. Community colleges — California’s open-door promise to anyone who wants an education — are also slipping out of reach for want of affordable housing.

In a 2025 state survey, about 20 percent of California community college students said they experienced homelessness, and nearly 60 percent reported housing insecurity.

When we leave student housing to the private market, we know which students get pushed out.

We need sustained public investment in affordable housing if public higher education is to remain one of our most powerful engines of social mobility. California took a giant step with the Higher Education Student Housing Grant program created in 2022 — a more than $2 billion commitment to affordable housing for low-income students in all three public segments — but more is needed. Investments in affordable housing solutions, like social housing, can also ensure housing stability for people while they are students and beyond.

A public university is open to everyone only if everyone has a place to live.

Jetaun StevensSacramentoThe writer is the deputy director for higher education and a senior staff attorney at Public Advocates, a civil rights law firm and advocacy organization based in California.

To the Editor:

Your article correctly points out that housing shortages around universities can cause pressure on the housing market and increase costs for both locals and students who may then need to go into debt to afford housing in addition to their base tuition.

While the universities should absolutely be providing housing for their students, they should be restricted from requiring that students under a certain age live in campus housing beyond the first year. Otherwise, it would be all too easy for university administrators to fix budget holes by extracting higher-than-market rents from contractually captive tenants.

James WalkerLos Osos, Calif.

To the Editor:

Re “Latino Voters Swing Back to Democrats, Again Reshaping Electoral Map” (news article, Nov. 7):

Both Democrats and Republicans profess shock at the dramatic swing of Hispanic voters away from the G.O.P. I’m shocked that anyone is shocked.

After two years of open Latino-bashing, ICE violence and arrests of law-abiding, long-term residents, family separations, third-country deportations, lack of due process, Supreme Court approval of racial profiling, attacks on birthright citizenship and intolerable conditions at deportation facilities, why would Hispanic voters ever trust the G.O.P. to treat that community fairly?

Of course they abandoned the party of deportation, cruelty and nativism. That’s not the America they (or the rest of us) want to live in.

Cheryl GreenbergWest Hartford, Conn.The writer is an emerita professor of history at Trinity College.

To the Editor:

Re “Justice Kagan Sounds an Alarm,” by Jesse Wegman (Opinion guest essay, Nov. 5):

Mr. Wegman agrees with Justice Elena Kagan that the Supreme Court’s legitimacy is important to its effectiveness and that this legitimacy “helps to create a stable country.” The problem is that the court, through its many unpopular opinions, has to a great extent lost this legitimacy. This is apparent in the court’s historically low approval rating with the American public. Mr. Wegman proposes that the solution is “major court reform imposed by Congress.”

I actually think there is a reasonable chance the court will take note of the public’s disapproval and begin to reform itself. I believe that a majority of the justices — including Chief Justice John Roberts — care about the court’s standing with the public and about their individual legacies.

I also think Justice Kagan’s is right that the originalism sometimes applied by today’s court is often “not a very good match with the Constitution we have.”

In fact, the founders themselves might not have agreed with it. Thomas Jefferson wrote — in words quoted on the wall of the Jefferson Memorial — that “laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind” and that as views and opinions change, “institutions must advance also to keep pace with the times.”

I hope the public’s and Justice Kagan’s dissatisfaction with the Supreme Court will not be lost on the other members of the court. The court’s continuing legitimacy may depend on it.

Walter SmithWashingtonThe writer is a lawyer who has argued cases before the Supreme Court and who practiced law with Chief Justice John Roberts before he joined the Supreme Court.

]]>
